detector_comparison.notes: Every detector hit appears twice in detectors.json (identical entries), so the 19 hits are about 10 distinct items. No SLP tells were reported, consistent with my reading: the page is tell-free but plain (zero tells is not the same as specific).

findings.title: No identity layer of the harbour's own: the visual frame is a swappable default booking form
findings.description: Across all five routes the only identity-carrying elements are the name in bold body sans and a stock anchor icon. Type voice, colour anchor (one dark teal), ground (pale grey-blue), shape and imagery are what any public-service booking form would have; swap, category-guess and similar-prompt tests all fail. The product's own world (tide, sill gate, pontoon plan, the harbour's physical colours) appears only in copy.
findings.impact: Skippers new to the harbour may not form any recognisable picture of Saltmarsh Quay from the booking flow, and the page is likely to read as unfinished rather than as the harbour's own service.

evidence.detail: first viewport: header, H1, native fields, teal button on flat ground

findings.recommendation: Write DESIGN.md first: decide attributes from the harbour's world and pick one signature that comes from its mechanism (the tide/sill-gate window is the obvious candidate) and carry it through the steps where arrival time matters; decide a name treatment and ground that belong to this place.

findings.title: Tide table, the one product-specific element, is set as an unstyled default table with misaligned column headers
findings.description: On the plan-visit page the 'Tide times' table has 'Morning' and 'Afternoon' headers left-aligned while their times are right-aligned at the far edge of each column, so each header floats away from its figures; the white table stops at 688px inside a wider column. This is the element that carries the product's difference (arrival by tide) and it is the least finished-looking part of the page.
findings.impact: Skippers scanning for the HW time on their arrival day may find the header-to-figure relationship slower to read, and the page's only distinctive content is likely to look like a placeholder.

evidence.detail: 'Morning' header at x≈391 left-aligned; '02:08' ends at x≈515 right-aligned

findings.recommendation: Decide one alignment rule for numeric columns and apply it to headers and cells together; decide whether this table is the product's signature and treat it accordingly.

findings.title: Wide layouts leave the right third empty and the footer stops mid-viewport on short pages
findings.description: At 1024–1440 every route keeps content in a column ending near 750px inside a ~1072px container, leaving a blank band on the right; on short pages (boat, review, confirmed, booking stopped) the white footer band ends partway down and a large empty grey field continues below it.
findings.impact: On desktop the pages are likely to look unfinished, with the footer reading as a band that stops short for no reason.

evidence.detail: footer ends at y≈476; empty ground below

findings.recommendation: Decide how the page frame behaves when content is short (footer anchored to the viewport bottom or ground matching the footer) and what the wide-width column is for.

findings.title: 'Change dates' is hidden behind an isolated kebab button that becomes the second thing seen on the berth page
findings.description: On choose-berth a lone '...' button sits at the far right of the container, detached from the H1 and the list, with an empty band beside it; it is the second fixation after the H1. It holds 'Change dates' (a core task) and 'Harbour rules'. When opened the menu pushes the berth list down rather than overlaying it.
findings.impact: Skippers who need to change their arrival date may not recognise an unlabelled '...' as the way to do it, while the button still draws the eye away from the berth list.

evidence.detail: menu open; list shifted from y≈293 to y≈407

findings.recommendation: Decide whether changing dates is part of the page's visible summary (next to 'Arriving on Saturday 17 October…') rather than an overflow action.

findings.title: Errored fields are marked inconsistently: some keep the default border
findings.description: In the boat errors state, 'Boat name', 'Draught' and 'MMSI' inputs get red borders but 'Length' keeps a dark default border despite its 'Enter the length' message. On plan-visit errors, 'Arrival date' turns red but the 'Arrival time' select keeps the default grey border despite 'Choose the time you plan to arrive'.
findings.impact: Skippers correcting errors, often on a phone in bright light, may miss a field whose error is shown only by text above it.

evidence.detail: Length input border dark, siblings red

findings.recommendation: Decide one error treatment for every control type (inputs and selects) and apply it from a shared state token.

findings.title: Arrival time and the sill-gate window drop out of review and confirmation
findings.description: The brief says the arrival time matters as much as the date because boats can only cross the sill around high water. Review shows 'Saturday 17 October 2026 at 15:00' with no gate window; confirmation shows 'Arrival: Saturday 17 October 2026' with no time at all. The tide information lives only on the first page.
findings.impact: Skippers keeping the confirmation to hand on arrival may not have the time they booked or the gate window in front of them, which is the one thing that distinguishes this harbour's booking.
findings.recommendation: Decide where the arrival time and gate window are shown through the flow; this is also the natural place for the product's signature.

findings.title: List heading 'Pontoon spaces free on these dates' also covers the wall berth
findings.description: The H1 'Choose a pontoon space' and the list label 'Pontoon spaces free on these dates' sit over four options, the last of which is 'Wall berth 2', which 'Settles on soft mud at low water' and is not a pontoon.
findings.impact: Skippers with boats over 12 metres, who the rules send to the wall berth, may think no suitable space is offered.
findings.recommendation: Decide a heading that names what the list actually contains.

findings.title: Headings and key values wrap to a single stranded word at phone widths
findings.description: At 320–375px several H1s break with one word on the second line ('Choose a pontoon / space', 'Check your mooring / booking'), and the dead-end message splits the reference as 'BK-' / '409.'. Phones are the main device.
findings.impact: Splitting a reference number across lines may cause a skipper to misread or mis-copy it when calling the harbour office; stranded heading words make the main device's view look less finished.

evidence.detail: corroborated by sealed detector TYP-15 hits

findings.recommendation: Decide a wrapping rule for headings and keep identifiers unbreakable.

strengths: Copy is plain, matter-of-fact and in the skipper's own terms ('Afloat at every state of the tide', 'Settles on soft mud at low water', 'You pay at the harbour office when you arrive. Nothing is charged online.').
Structure is conventional and calm for Operate surfaces: one H1, one primary action per page, error summary with linked messages, generous touch-sized controls at 320px.
Tide times with the sill-gate rule are presented next to the date choice, which is the right place for the product's key constraint.
keep: Keep the plain, specific harbour copy and the one-primary-action-per-step structure; add identity and a signature without adding steps or decoration to the forms.
not_assessable: Brand fit (DES-04): DESIGN.md missing, no attributes declared.
Dark theme: not captured; context mentions night use, so its absence is a gap in the matrix rather than a judgement.
Focus, selected-card, hover and menu behaviour cannot be judged from stills.
